newsitem.title: USA: WebTV, facing competition, to add new features.
newsitem.headline: WebTV, facing competition, to add new features.

text.p: WebTV Networks Inc., facing increased competition from new entrants and awaiting approval of a $425 million buyout, said Tuesday it will offer a flurry of new services at no extra cost.

WebTV said it will deliver a free software upgrade by the end of the month which will include support for secure online transactions, printing capabilities and features which will enhance the use of multimedia formats.

Following some industry criticism of the company's closed system strategy, in which it has required users of its set-top box to subscribe to its service, even when it involves costly long-distance calls, the company said it will allow customers to use any compatible provider.

WebTV said this will be particularly useful for people who already have a provider for their personal computer which they prefer to use - customers will be billed $9.95 monthly for this, $10 a month below WebTV's network.
WebTV also said it was providing an electronic television programming guide, complete with listings in their area and data about their favorite celebrities.

The news may help cheer WebTV's over 85,000 customers, some of whom have complained in electronic postings at the length of time it has taken to upgrade the system and about persistent problems with equipment shutting off.
The set-top boxes are sold by WebTV partners Sony Corp. and Philips Electronics NV.
WebTV said customer satisfaction levels have exceeded 90 percent, according to its polling statistics, and that 67 percent of WebTV subscribers connect to the Internet through WebTV Network each day.
Subscribers will be able to print e-mail, photographs, news articles and Web pages using an add-on connection to Hewlett-Packard Co.'s HP DeskJet 400 series prtiners and 600 series color printers.

The company also said it was supplying Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) support for secure Internet transactions, along with new multimedia features, such as improved audio and graphics animation support, and personalization.

On April 6, Microsoft Corp. announced it had signed a definitive agreement to acquire WebTV in a deal valued at the time at $425 million. The deal is subject to regulatory approval and has not received a go-ahead.

Last month a flood of companies announced plans to provide products and services to enable people to access the Internet conveniently from their televisions - all before WebTV could disclose hitting the 100,000 user mark.

These include NetChannel, Inc., which said it has inked a deal with Thomson Consumer Electronics to provide an Internet delivery service for $19.95 a month and plans to offer $300 set-top boxes from this autumn.

A third Internet access network, Los Gatos, Calif.- based ICTV Inc., connects a keyboard to a small set-top box and a television set to provide access to Internet and to video games through a cable television connection.
Privately-held ICTV has also inked a deal with General Instruments Corp and its investors include Cox Communications, International Business Machines Corp. and Lauder Investments.

Semiconductor maker Zilog and privately-held software company PlanetWeb are teaming up to unveil a design which will allow manufacturers to build set-top boxes to sell at street prices of less than $200.
This is $50 less than current prices of WebTV units.

Curtis Mathes Holding, a Dallas, Texas-based television manufacturer, has also unveiled a $400 set-top box which turns a TV into a fax machine and speaker phone in addition to an Internet and electronic mail device.

Microsoft vice president of corporate development and treasurer Greg Maffei acknowledged at a Red Herring venture capital investment conference in Monterey, Calif., last month Microsoft had paid a rich valuation for WebTV, but added that for the software giant it was a play on the convergence of computers and television entertainment.
"WebTV isn't the only solution, but we think it offers some pretty cool options," Maffei said at the time. "Their tagline -- it just works -- is very cool."
(sam.perry@reuters.com, in Palo Alto, +1 415 846 5400)
